full_judgment:
AKM Abdul Hakim J: This application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, has been filed seeking quashment of the proceedings of Sessions Case No. 561 of 2010 under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 arising out of CR Case No. 843 of 2009 now pending before the learned Metropolitan Additional. Sessions Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong. 

 2. The case of the Complainant-opposite party No. 2, in short, is that the complainant has filed a petition of complaint against the accused-petitioner before Metropolitan Magistrate, 3rd Court, Chittagong under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act,1881 (shortly, the NI Act) alleging; inter alia, that accused-petitioner purchased a sunken ship, namely "Royal Bird" from the complainant for a total consideration of Taka 11,00,000 only and out of total consideration accused-petitioner paid a sum of Taka 6,50,000 by issuing 3(three) cheques being Nos. 8877938 dated 30-11-2008 for Taka 2,50,000 Nos.8877939 dated 15-12-2008 for Taka 2,00,000 and Nos. 8877940 dated 30-12-2008 for Taka 2,00,000 drawn on Public Bank Limited, Port Branch, Chittagong against Current Account No 3115. The cheques were deposited on 21-5-2009 in the complainant's account maintained in the ICB Islami Bank Ltd, Narayangonj Branch and presented for clearance before the respective Bank but the same were dishonoured for insufficient funds. Thereafter the complainant issued a legal notice on 16-6-2009 under section 138 of the Negotiable Instrument Act, 1881 demanding payment of Taka 6,50,000 being due under the aforesaid three cheques within 30 days from the receipt of the legal notice. Since no payment was made, the complainant filed a petition of complaint before the Metropolitan Magistrate 3rd Court, Chittagong on 12-8-2009. 

 4. Then the case was transmitted to the Metropolitan Sessions Judge Court, Chittagong and registered as Sessions Case No.561 of 2010 and consequently the case was sent to the Additional Metropolitan Sessions Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong for trial. The learned Metropolitan Additional Sessions judge Chittagong framed charge on 25-4-2010 under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. At the time of framing charge the accused-petitioner was not present in the Court as such learned Additional Sessions Judge issued warrant of arrest. The accused-petitioner then surrendered before the Court on 24-5-2010 and obtained bail. 

 10. He further submits that since the question raised in the petition of complaint in respect of non-disclosure the date of dishonoured cheques is a question of fact to be easily ascertained at the time of trial after taking evidence. Non-disclosure of such fact in the complaint-petition cannot render the proceeding liable to be quashed to the great prejudice of the complainant who is entitled to prove the case on evidence. In support of his contention learned Advocate for the opposite party referred to the case of Nizamuddin Mahmood vs Abdul Hamid Bhuiyan reported in 60 DLR (AD) 195. 

 13. Mr Md Ali Jinnah, the learned Assistant Attorney General appearing on behalf of the state-opposite-party No.1 by adopting the submissions advanced by the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 2 submits that the present petition has been initiated for a collateral purpose just to delay in disposal of the case pending before the trial and not to secure ends of justice. As such, the accused-petitioner has not come before this Court in clean hands and is not entitled to get relief under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 14. He further submits that jurisdiction of the High Court Division under section 561A of Code is taken resort to only when there is no other remedy. Since the Petitioner has remedy before this Honourable Court by way of a revisional application or at the time of framing charge and agitate the question raised hereto to correct the alleged mistake. In the facts and circumstance of the case an application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is prima-facie not maintainable. In this respect the learned Assistant Attorney General referred a decision in the case of Maksudur Rahman Hilaly vs State, reported in 47 DLR 314. 

 15. The main question to be decided in the case is whether for non-mentioning the date of dishonoured three cheques in the petition of complaint whether the proceedings should be quashed; whether the petitioner filed the case satisfying the provisions of law; whether taking cognizance of the offences in this case is in contravention of law and whether the continuation of proceedings under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 amounts to an abuse of the process of the Court. 

 17. In order to appreciate the points raised in the present case, we need to examine section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. Section 138 provides for punishment for dishonor of cheque for insufficiency; etc. Of funds in the account, which runs under: 

 (b) The payee or the holder in due course of the cheque , as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice, in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid, and 

 (c) The drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within (thirty days) of the receipt of the said notice." 

 (a) no Court shall take cognizance of any offence punishable under section 138 except upon a complaint, in writing, made by the payee or, as the case may be, the holder in due course of the cheque: 

 20. Thereafter, considering sub-section (1) of section 138 along with clause (b) of section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, it appears that clause (b) of section 141 makes provision for filing the complaint within one month of the date on which the "cause of action" arose under clause (c) of the proviso to section 138(1) of the Act. Apparently, this sections 138 and 141 also does not contemplate more than one cause of action, while it is now settled that cause of action under clause (c) of section 138 (1) arises once the payee fails to pay amount demanded within 30 days of receiving the notices. Rather clause (b) of section 141, read with sub-section (1) of section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, clearly signifies that dishonour of a cheque per se would not bring drawer of the dishonoured cheque within the mischief of sub-section (1) of the section 138. There must have arisen a cause of action for taking cognizance under clause (b) of section 141 of the Act. Such cause of action arises upon failure of the drawer of cheque to make payment of "the amount of money", within 30 days of receiving the notice deman-ding payment of the amount under the dishonoured cheque and not within 30 days of dishonour of a cheque. 

 23. In the present case, since, in the demand notice the total amount of the 3 (three) cheques amounting to Taka 6,50,000 has been demanded and the drawer of the cheque having failed to make payment of the "said amount of money" within 30 days, only one cause of action has arisen and, legally, for one cause of action there should be one complaint petition, which has exactly been done in the impugned proceeding. As such, we do not find any illegally or any abuse of the process of the Court in issuing a single notice for 3(three) cheques, as because notice has been served and the demand has been made within the stipulated period of time. We also find support of our view in the case of Zahid Hossain vs State reported in 61 DLR 386 in which the complainant issued a single notice of demand for 8 (eight) dishonoured cheques and initiated a single proceeding and the petition for quashment challenging the said proceedings filed. 

 25. The learned Advocate for the petitioner once again gave emphasis that the complainant did not mention the date of dishonoured cheques in the petition of complainant. Whether the complainant mentioned the date of dishonoured cheques or not, it is merely a disputed question of fact and same should be decided in the trial after taking evidence. The plea of the accused is nothing but defence plea. Be that as it may, the proposition of law is now well settled that on the basis of the defence plea or materials criminal proceedings should not be stifled before trial, when there is a prima-facie case for going for trial. In such view of the matter submissions advanced by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is repelled as the same are devoid of any substance. In this connection reference may be made in case of Rahela Khatun vs Abul Hassan reported in 48 DLR (AD) 213. 

 26. Furthermore, the cause of action of a criminal case should be ascertained in its entirety, that is, from the initiation of the proceedings to its ends. For the reason of non-mentioning the date of dishonoured cheques in the petition of complainant, the course of justice should not be interrupted readily and proceedings should not be quashed. 

 27. There is nothing in the four corners of section 138 or of section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act that for non-mentioning of receiving date of the legal notice in the petition of complaint, the case will be rendered illegal when all other ingredients in filing the case is very much available in the materials on record. We find support of above view in the case of Nizamuddin Mahmood vs Abdul Hamid Bhuiyan reported in 60 DLR (AD) 195. In the said decision their Lordships held: 

 "Since the date of receipt is a question of fact to be ascertained at the time of trial, non-disclosure of such fact in the complaint petition cannot render the proceeding liable to be quashed to the great prejudice of the complainant who is entitled to prove his case on evidence." 

 28. In view of the decision of our apex Court we are of the opinion that failure to mention the date of dishonoured cheques in the petition of complaint is a question of fact to be ascertained at the time of trial after taking evidence and thus non mentioning of such fact in the complaint petition cannot rendered the proceeding liable to be quashed to the great prejudice of the complainant who is entitled to prove his case on evidence. 

 31. It further appears that in view of failure to mention disclose the date of dishonour of the cheques in the complaint petition and such a fact is to be proved at the trial after taking evidence and therefore, such a question cannot be decided in a proceeding under section 561A of the Court of Criminal Procedure in view of the decision of our apex Court in the case of Abdul Kader Chowdhury vs State reported in 28 DLR (AD) 38 wherein it was held that where assessment of evidence is involved the case cannot quashed. 

 32. We have examined the decision reported in 60 DLR (AD) 195 cited by the learned Advocate for the opposite-party No. 2. We are of the opinion that the principle enunciated in the said case is fully applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case. 

 33. In the facts and circumstances of the present case and the decisions quoted above, we are of the view that dishonour of cheque for insufficiency of fund is an offence under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act which prima-facie appears from the petition of complaint to have been committed by the petitioner. There is no valid ground for quashing the proceeding under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act against the petitioner. Since there being existence of ingredient for proceeding with the criminal case, the application for quashment is misconceived and same does not warrant interference under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
